stories.headline: FBI investigates apparent hack of its national crime database
stories.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, the database police across the country use to check for fugitives, missing persons, criminal histories and stolen property, according to an Associated Press report citing a single source. President Trump said Saturday the breach was "not good" but could let the government learn things it otherwise would not have. What was taken, and by whom, has not been made public in the coverage available.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the system an officer queries during a traffic stop or a missing-person search, and it holds sensitive records about millions of people. A breach could expose personal data or undermine confidence in records that police rely on every day.
stories.background: The National Crime Information Center, or NCIC, is a computerized index run by the FBI and shared with local, state and federal law enforcement. It began operating in 1967 and covers wanted persons, missing persons, criminal history data and stolen property. The FBI has disclosed other security incidents this year: in September it said it was investigating a hacking group's claim to have stolen employee data through its jobs website. CNBC described the NCIC incident as the second recent intrusion into FBI systems.

facts.text: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database, the Associated Press reported, citing a source.
The NCIC is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal histories and stolen property.
Trump said Saturday in a phone interview that the potential breach was "not good" but might be a chance to "learn things that we would have never learned otherwise."
CNBC reported this would be the second recent intrusion into FBI systems.
In September the FBI said it was investigating a criminal hacking group's claim to have stolen sensitive data on agents and job applicants through its jobs website.
The NCIC began operating in January 1967, according to the FBI.

stories.headline: Trump orders federal contractors to consult White House before answering Congress
stories.summary: President Trump signed an executive order Saturday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold communications the White House considers privileged. The White House warned that companies that do not comply could lose their contracts and be suspended from future federal work. The order comes weeks before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
stories.why_it_matters: Private companies do a large share of the government's work, and Congress often learns how taxpayer money is spent by asking them directly. The order could limit what lawmakers, and through them the public, find out. In today's ingest the story was carried almost entirely by left-leaning and center outlets.
stories.background: Democrats won control of Congress in this month's midterm elections and are expected to open wide-ranging investigations of the administration when they take over in January. Congressional committees can request or subpoena documents from companies that hold federal contracts. Presidents can claim executive privilege to keep some internal communications from Congress, and disputes over its reach are usually settled by negotiation or in court. Several outlets describe the order as the administration's latest step to resist that expected oversight.

facts.text: Trump directed federal contractors and subcontractors to consult his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold communications the White House considers privileged.
The White House warned that contractors who fail to comply could have their contracts terminated and their future federal work suspended, CBS News reported.

stories.headline: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card rates at 10%
stories.summary: President Trump said Saturday he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, repeating a call he first made in January. He said in a phone interview that card companies make too much money and that he "would do it." No bill or timetable was reported.
stories.why_it_matters: The typical card rate is around 22%, so a 10% cap would sharply cut interest costs for people who carry a balance. Banks have argued a cap would lead them to offer less credit, especially to riskier borrowers.
stories.background: Trump called in January for a one-year, 10% cap on credit card interest and later asked Congress to pass it, but no cap took effect. Sens. Bernie Sanders and Josh Hawley had earlier introduced a bipartisan bill for a 10% cap. Banking groups opposed the idea, saying it would reduce access to credit. Democrats won control of Congress in this month's midterms and take over in January.

facts.text: Trump said Saturday he would work with Democrats in the incoming Congress to cap credit card interest rates at 10%.
Axios reported Trump said he would also cap card fees and argued card companies make too much money.
"They've been trying to get that for years. I would do it," Trump said of Democrats in a phone interview, according to The Hill.
The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
Trump first called for a one-year 10% cap in January.

stories.headline: Immigration officers arrest two passengers on Seattle airport jet bridge
stories.summary: Masked immigration officers arrested two people on a crowded jet bridge at Seattle's airport Saturday as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, delaying the flight. Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle both called the scene distressing, and the port said local authorities would ask federal officials what happened. Washington's governor also criticized the arrests, The New York Times reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Arrests in the boarding area of a commercial flight put ordinary travelers in the middle of an enforcement action and raise questions about where immigration arrests take place. The airport's operator says it has no control over federal immigration officers on its property.
stories.background: The Trump administration has stepped up immigration enforcement nationwide, and attorneys said earlier this year that arrests at airports were becoming more frequent. Seattle-Tacoma International Airport is run by the Port of Seattle, a local public agency that says it has no jurisdiction over Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations there.

facts.text: Masked immigration officers arrested two people on a crowded jet bridge in Seattle on Saturday while passengers were boarding.
The arrests delayed the Los Angeles-bound Alaska Airlines flight.
Alaska Airlines called the scene "distressing" for passengers and employees.
The Port of Seattle said the arrest was distressing for the affected family and other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

The Port of Seattle says it has no jurisdiction over ICE operations at the airport.
Immigration attorneys said in July that ICE arrests at U.S. airports were happening more often, CNN reported.

stories.headline: Appeals court says law protecting pregnant workers was passed unconstitutionally
stories.summary: The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a law protecting pregnant workers was passed unconstitutionally because House members voted by proxy during the Covid pandemic, The New York Times reported. The ruling halts the law, and the case is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court. CNN and The Washington Post described the decision as striking at the wider spending law that contained the protections.
stories.why_it_matters: The law requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for pregnant workers, and those protections are now in question. The reasoning could also be used to challenge other laws passed while the House allowed proxy voting. Only left-leaning outlets in today's ingest covered the ruling.
stories.background: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was passed at the end of 2022 as part of a large government spending bill, at a time when House rules let absent members cast votes through colleagues. Texas sued, arguing that the Constitution requires a majority of members to be physically present to pass legislation. A federal judge in Texas agreed in 2024 and blocked the law's enforcement against the state as an employer. A three-judge Fifth Circuit panel reversed that decision in August 2025, and the court then took up the case again.

facts.text: The Fifth Circuit said the law was unconstitutional because it was passed with proxy voting during the Covid pandemic, The New York Times reported.
The decision is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court, according to The New York Times.
A Fifth Circuit panel had ruled in August 2025 that the House's use of proxy voting did not violate the Constitution's quorum requirement.
A federal judge in Texas had earlier blocked enforcement of the law against the state of Texas as an employer.

stories.headline: Storms on both coasts threaten Thanksgiving travel as San Francisco braces for record tides
stories.summary: San Francisco's mayor asked residents not to travel unless "absolutely essential" as Northern California prepares for heavy rain arriving with unusually high tides. In central Florida, more rain is falling on areas already hit by flooding that the Associated Press described as historic, and a storm moving up the East Coast could also delay holiday travel.
stories.why_it_matters: Thanksgiving week is one of the busiest travel periods of the year, and storms on both coasts could mean flight delays, closed roads and flooded neighborhoods for millions of people.
stories.background: This is an El Niño winter, a pattern that tends to bring wetter weather to California. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie declared a local emergency in October to prepare for it. King tides, the highest tides of the year, were forecast to peak in the Bay Area around Thanksgiving, and local reporting had warned they could coincide with a storm. Florida has separately been dealing with flooding from a major storm system.

facts.text: San Francisco's mayor asked people in the city not to travel unless "absolutely essential."
Northern California is preparing for heavy rain accompanied by high tides ahead of Thanksgiving, while scattered rain is worsening flooding across central Florida.
A storm moving up the Eastern seaboard could also cause travel delays before the holiday, NPR reported.
Entire neighborhoods in parts of Florida are underwater after a major storm system brought heavy rain, NBC News reported.
The mayor described the expected king tides as "never-before-seen," according to CNN.

KQED reported earlier this month that extreme king tides were expected in the Bay Area around Thanksgiving.

stories.headline: Jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire
stories.summary: A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty of arson charges for starting the January 2025 Palisades Fire, which killed 12 people. It was his second trial; the first ended in a mistrial earlier this year. France 24 reported he faces between five and 40 years in prison.
stories.why_it_matters: The fire was one of the most destructive in Los Angeles history, and the verdict is a formal finding of who was responsible for a disaster that destroyed thousands of homes.
stories.background: The Palisades Fire broke out in January 2025 and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in and around the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles. Federal prosecutors charged Rinderknecht, a former rideshare driver, with arson. His first trial ended in June when the jury deadlocked, with 10 of 12 jurors favoring acquittal according to the Associated Press, and the judge set a retrial at prosecutors' request.

facts.text: A federal jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of arson charges Friday for starting the 2025 Palisades Fire.
